title: Improving Trauma Care Act of 2014
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was reported to the House on May 20, 2014. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Improving Trauma Care Act of 2014 - Amends the Public Health Service Act to include in the definition of "trauma" injuries resulting from thermal, electrical, chemical, or radioactive agents, thus making burn centers eligible for trauma center grants and trauma research programs.

summary.headline: A 2014 law adds burn injuries from heat, electricity, chemicals, or radiation to the federal definition of trauma, so burn centers can qualify for trauma grants and research.
summary.what_it_does: The law changes the Public Health Service Act. Before, the federal definition of "trauma" did not clearly cover some injuries, such as burns from heat, electricity, chemicals, or radioactive materials. Under the law, those injuries count as trauma. As a result, burn centers can now apply for federal trauma center grants and take part in federal trauma research programs.

who_it_affects.how: They can now be considered for federal trauma center grants and trauma research programs.
Facilities that treat severe burns may compete for federal trauma funding under the broader definition.

who_it_affects.group: People with severe burns or injuries from electrical, chemical, or radioactive agents
who_it_affects.how: Federal trauma programs now cover these injuries, which may affect the care resources available to them.
Researchers studying burn and related injuries can apply for federal trauma research funding.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted on August 8, 2014, and the official summary does not list a separate effective date for this change.
